newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Yield Spreads-Shows tighter bias to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Australia Yield Spreads-Shows tighter bias to U.S..

text.p: Australian bonds showed a mild outperforming bias against the U.S., reversing some of the spread widening seen late on Monday.

U.S. Treasuries lost ground in Tokyo trading, erasing some of the bullishness in New York when asset allocation switching from U.S. stocks was seen when it looked like the Dow Jones industrial average was going to take another deep dive.

Local yields seesawed either side of Monday's close in immediate response to the Reserve Bank's August Bulletin, but later edged higher when it was clear that it contained little new than what governor Macfarlane had said in Perth last week.

In the report, the RBA said the narrow differential between long-term bond yields in Australia and the U.S. suggested confidence that Australia would sustain the recent performance on inflation beyond the medium term.
Noting that the spread had recently touched its lowest level since August 1984, it said it signified a much healthier state of affairs than the situation of the mid 1980s
"In 1984, bond yields both in the United States and Australia were around 13-14 percent, with U.S. yields having increased as U.S. inflation expectations deteriorated," it said.
"The recent experience has seen bond yields in Australia fall toward those in the United States, based on comparably low inflation rates," the RBA added.
Australian annual headline inflation was 0.3 percent in the second quarter compared with annual U.S. inflation of 2.2 percent in July.
Meanwhile, the negative spread to New Zealand widened again.
NZ debt remained under pressure as the fragility of the NZ dollar continued to weigh on the market.
